I was just thinking about games, and how they affect people. I had a class a few months back where we were asked what makes a game "realistic" or "real". A lot of the answers were about graphics, or simulation, and they were put into different categories on this board. My answer was unrelated to these. To me, a game becomes real when it affects you in real life. When you start to think about something a different way, or consider something you'd never thought of before. When you're emotionally affected by it. It's like the game leaping off of the screen and into the real world. Even if it's only in a small way, to me, that's a game being real; changing the world. Like a game I played, Digital Devil Saga 2. When the characters triumphed, I was happy. When characters died, I was said. When it was all over, I wished there were more. To me, that makes it real.

What about you? Have you ever been moved by a game? What was it?

Spiritual is a pretty meaningless word to me, but if it means anything than it is a good description of my experience playing Journey. Jason Rohrers Passage. It's free to download and the game is strictly limited to ~5 minutes of playtime. In that time you will move a person through their entire life from early childhood to death. The CEO of Ubisoft at one point said that this game made him cry and he felt bitter that his gigantic studio was not able to produce something this meaningful (mind you, this was some time ago, before the U-Play cancer, so don't get your hopes it that Ubi might become good guys again).

Then there was Braid by Jonathan Blow, which I hope most people have played by now. I am still searching for a game this deep and meaningful. The entire point of this game is to inflict emotional meaning onto you through gameplay and the context you create through your actions. This is the first (and so far only) game where I experienced that game play mechanics were a device of storytelling that irrefutably justified the existence of interactive media. You simply cannot tell the story of Braid without the game play. Not with different gameplay and not without its gameplay. A book or film or music or theatre would not be able to narrate this story , the only way to experience it outside of the game would be if this particular journey would actually happen to you in person and you would be involved in its telling.

Braid affected me emotionally in a way that I wasn't able to explain for a long time. It did change my perspective as it gave me the chance to intuitively understand a series of choices and a journey that I will hopefully never face in real life.

Preface: I identify as an everything. Feminist, MRA, egalitarian, whatever. I'm pro-equality. I am confused about what I think about nearly everything, and I think every gender issues movement has teaspoon of sugar and shovel full of shit.

I have been reading more men's rights stuff, and I think there are many valid points. I believe that most of men's privileges come at a very high cost, and I have a rather different understanding of patriarchy than most feminists. In fact, I rather hate the word patriarchy, as so many feminists use it to ignore reality and focus instead on confirmation bias. But assholes can still be right. So my rather uninformed view has so far led me to the conclusion that inequality between the sexes occurs mostly when one sex wanders into a space that traditionally belonged to the other. Men often face prejudice in becoming a nurturing or the primary parent. Women face prejudice in taking on highly technical or difficult jobs that have been male-dominated.

But one of these is a more serious obstacle than the other. And one is far more about power and influence than the other. While in some ways women have gotten enormous amounts of power, and they certainly seem to have much cultural control over certain things, I can't understand how men's inequalities regarding power and influence are as significant as those of women. Women have less representation nearly everywhere, are often less heard, and even in progressive cultures like that of academia often have to face absurd, sexist treatment that I wouldn't believe if I hadn't heard so many stories from my academic friends.

Explicit sexism or bigotry is very rare among anyone. We can sometimes see it in law or crazy fringe people, but the majority of sexism against both men and women is implicit. This can be seen in male disposability, for example, which very few people would admit to believing in, but many still demonstrate their belief through action. To be perfectly clear, I think this particular issue is a huge problem. I don't understand why so many feminists don't understand why MRAs make such a large deal out of the draft. That's a big deal.

But what about the implicit message we send so often that we don't care about the female perspective? Stand up comics talking about male issues are for everyone, but comics talking about female issues are predominately for women. Music from a male perspective is for everyone, but much of music from a female perspective is for women. And how much of media does this apply to? A lot. Movies. Books. Sports (Men's sports is for our entertainment, we care about it, women's sports is often thought of as doing the athletes a favor). Constantly sending the message that your ideas don't matter, no one cares what you have to say, and aren't you cute thinking you'll actually influence the world, and all of this because of your sex of all the asinine reasons, is a pretty big fucking issue.

And women in many ways have less influence and power, and their attempts to enter these arenas are often met with resistance. I think this resistance is often unintentional and a result of traditional gender roles that will no doubt change with time, but whether deliberated or not, the pushback has the same effect.

This post is far from comprehensive, but listing all the major inequalities men and women face would be a project. And I would like to clarify that men could still have it off worse, but have more power. The point of patriarchy, from my perspective at least, isn't to say that women deliberately are more oppressed/have it off worse/blah blah blah. I have zero interest in the oppression wars. My point isn't to say that women are less likely to be happy or that they face more problems than men, but only to say that it is on average easier for a man to gain power and influence than a woman.
